item.title: 200kW-class heavy-fuel aircraft engine to be unveiled at Zhuhai airshow
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 22:20:00
Yousun DB626 engine (190kW) Photo: Anhui Haery Aviation Power Co Ltd A Chinese aircraft engine manufacturer will showcase a new 200kW-class heavy-fuel piston engine at an upcoming international airshow in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province, highlighting the continued development of domestically produced propulsion systems for unmanned aircraft. Anhui Haery Aviation Power Co Ltd (also known as Hangrui Power in China) will officially exhibit its new Yousun DB626 engine at the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, according to the company. The exhibition, also known as Airshow China, is set to run from December 7 to 13, 2026. The engine is based on Haery's existing DB416 platform, but features a six-cylinder configuration instead of four cylinders. The company describes it as a new power option for larger unmanned aircraft and general aviation platforms. The DB626 adopts a horizontally opposed, six-cylinder, four-stroke, liquid-cooled configuration. Its core systems, including the single-cylinder combustion system, fuel injection system, full-authority digital engine control system (FADEC) and liquid-cooling system, are shared with the DB416, according to the manufacturer. Rather than developing an entirely new engine architecture, Haery has expanded the existing platform by adding two cylinders and increasing displacement. The approach allows the new model to build on technologies already used in the DB416 while extending the platform's power output, the company said. The DB626 retains the heavy-fuel compression-ignition technology used in the DB416 and can operate on diesel as well as RP-3 and RP-5 aviation kerosene. It is also equipped with a high-pressure common-rail fuel injection system and a turbocharged, intercooled intake system. Its FADEC system is designed to monitor engine operating conditions and provide an interface with aircraft flight control systems, the manufacturer said. Haery has also outlined a range of operating environments for the new engine, including high-altitude regions, maritime operations, cargo transportation and emergency response. The company said that the DB626 can maintain its continuous power output at an altitude of 4,000 meters, with a maximum operating altitude of 12,000 meters. It is designed to operate in temperatures ranging from -40 C to 71 C, while its stated time between overhauls exceeds 1,000 hours. The DB626's development comes as China expands the application of unmanned aircraft beyond traditional aerial observation and surveying toward cargo transportation, emergency services and other commercial operations. The availability of suitable domestic engines is an important part of supporting this expansion, particularly for platforms requiring longer endurance and heavier payloads. Haery's previous engine applications offer a glimpse into the role of domestic heavy-fuel propulsion systems in China's unmanned aviation sector, including their integration into military UAV platforms. In August 2022, a heavy-fuel version of China's CH-4 Rainbow unmanned aerial vehicle completed a series of flight tests after having replaced its original engine with a domestically developed heavy-fuel engine. The upgraded aircraft completed tests covering autonomous takeoff and landing, waypoint navigation, full-payload transportation, maximum service ceiling and flight endurance, according to China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC). The aircraft was developed by its subsidiary Aerospace CH UAV Co, Ltd. A subsequent report by the Anhui-based Dajiang News identified the engine as Haery's DB416 Yunque model, developed with independent intellectual property rights and domestic production capabilities. The CH-4 is one of China's best-known medium-altitude reconnaissance and strike UAV platforms. The aircraft is designed for long-endurance operations and can carry reconnaissance equipment as well as precision-guided weapons. Its upgraded heavy-fuel version was intended to improve endurance, payload capacity and operating performance in challenging environments. The integration of the DB416 into the CH-4 also represented a step forward for domestic propulsion-system development for a major Chinese UAV platform, according to the media reports. The Rainbow UAV family has developed into a broader product portfolio, with models serving different operational requirements. According to Rainbow UAV's annual report, the company's aircraft products have applications in both defense and civilian sectors. Beyond military missions, the platforms have also been developed for resource exploration, maritime monitoring, emergency response, forest fire prevention, communications and meteorological observation. Haery's heavy-fuel engines have also found applications in China's emerging commercial unmanned aviation sector. In April, the HH-200 commercial unmanned transport aircraft, developed by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), completed its maiden flight powered by two DB442 heavy-fuel piston engines made by Haery, according to a report by the local Wuhu News. The HH-200 is designed for cargo transportation, with a planned payload capacity of 1,000 kilograms and a range of 1,000 kilometers. Its maiden flight provided another example of domestically developed heavy-fuel engines being integrated into larger unmanned aircraft, extending their applications beyond reconnaissance and other defense-related missions into commercial logistics. The upcoming Airshow China will offer an opportunity to examine the latest developments in the company's engine portfolio, as China's aviation industry continues to explore domestic propulsion solutions for a wider range of unmanned aircraft applications. More than 1,100 companies from nearly 50 countries and regions are expected to participate in the 16th Airshow China, according to the Xinhua News Agency.

item.title: Chinese naval vessels, tanks arrive in Ream as China-Cambodia 'Golden Dragon-2026' exercise preparations advance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 21:25:00
Three PLA Navy vessels, the Type 071 amphibious landing ship Kunlunshan (Hull 998), the Type 054A guided-missile frigate Xuchang (Hull 536) and the Type 903A comprehensive replenishment ship Wulunguhu (Hull 893), dock at the Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream, Cambodia. Photo: PLA Southern Theater Command Preparations for the "Golden Dragon 2026" joint exercise between the Chinese and Cambodian militaries are progressing steadily at the Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream, the PLA Southern Theater Command said on Tuesday, releasing photos that showed several naval vessels and main battle tanks arriving at the center. The Chinese and Cambodian militaries will hold the 8th "Golden Dragon-2026" joint exercise in Cambodia from late November to mid-December, focusing on counterterrorism, anti-piracy and humanitarian rescue operations, China's Ministry of National Defense announced on Tuesday. Preparations have been proceeding smoothly since Chinese troops arrived at the Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center in Ream on November 22, with Chinese and Cambodian forces working in close coordination, the Southern Theater Command said. The photos showed three Chinese naval vessels at the Port Ream center: the Kunlunshan (Hull 998), a Type 071 amphibious landing ship; the Xuchang (Hull 536), a Type 054A guided-missile frigate; and the Wulunguhu (Hull 893), a Type 903A comprehensive replenishment ship. The images also showed Type 96 main battle tanks carried aboard the Kunlunshan disembarking. Type 96 main battle tanks disembarks from the Kunlunshan. Photo: PLA Southern Theater Command The exercise is scheduled to include familiarization training, command-post exercises and comprehensive live-force drills. After arriving in Cambodia, Chinese participating forces from the PLA Army, Navy, Air Force and Joint Logistics Support Force quickly moved by road to their designated deployment areas, while Chinese and Cambodian command elements stepped up preparations - coordinating operational plans, conducting site inspections and carrying out joint communications tests, according to the Southern Theater Command. The exercise will play a positive role in the building of an all-weather China-Cambodia community with a shared future in the new era, China's Ministry of National Defense said. The Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center was officially put into operation on April 5, 2025, according to the Xinhua News Agency. At the inauguration ceremony, both sides emphasized that the center was built and operates on the basis of mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Cambodia, which helps strengthening the practical cooperation, better fulfill international obligations and provide international public security goods. Alongside the ceremony, the Chinese and Cambodian militaries launched the "Golden Dragon 2025" joint exercise at the center, with vessels of both sides conducting in formation maneuvers, maritime communications, and equipment exercises. item.title: China's plateau border troops shift from stockpiling winter supplies to dynamic delivery
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 21:22:00
Photo: PLA Daily China's plateau border troops are moving away from the traditional practice of stockpiling large quantities of winter supplies toward a more flexible system based on on-demand procurement and cold-chain delivery, as improved infrastructure and supply-chain services reshape logistical support for troops stationed in remote, high-altitude areas, the PLA Daily reported on Tuesday. Recently, Wu Wengui, a quartermaster at a border defense company of the Chinese PLA Army, placed an order for winter supplies through an online platform dedicated to the regional procurement of food and other daily necessities. "Suppliers now handle centralized procurement and quality inspections, before delivering the supplies directly to border outposts through cold-chain transportation. Some items go straight to the kitchens, while the rest are temporarily stored in vegetable cellars," Wu told the PLA Daily. "Winter preparations have become much easier and faster, with supplies purchased according to demand through a single online order," Wu said. In the past, winter preparations for troops stationed on the plateau largely relied on stockpiling physical supplies before the onset of winter. Due to harsh weather and difficult road conditions, soldiers had to secure sufficient quantities of fuel, coal, rice, flour, cooking oil and other food supplies in advance to last through the winter. At the time, the amount of supplies stored in warehouses and the capacity of vegetable cellars were important measures of how well units had prepared for the cold season. That approach is now gradually giving way to a more dynamic model. As border road infrastructure continues to improve, cold-chain delivery vehicles can reach field locations directly, allowing supplies to be replenished as needed rather than stored in large quantities ahead of winter. As a result, many high-altitude outposts are no longer as constrained by traditional seasonal road closures. Shorter transportation times have also reduced food spoilage and losses, while fresh ingredients are increasingly appearing on delivery lists. With improved road conditions, the prolonged periods of road closures caused by heavy snowfall have largely become a thing of the past. The main challenge now is how to deal with delivery delays caused by temporary snow-related road closures, according to the report. When roads are open, refrigerated trucks deliver supplies to the outposts weekly. When roads are blocked, fresh leafy vegetables grown in greenhouses, together with emergency reserves kept in storage, help ensure that the quality of meals for troops remains unaffected. Alongside improvements in transportation, the supply network has also been expanded and made more resilient. Models including centralized regional procurement of food supplies, supplier-managed storage and contract-based reserves are being introduced more widely, enabling troops to place orders online while suppliers arrange the necessary goods and deliver them directly through cold-chain networks. The shift means that instead of individual units having to store everything themselves, more resources can be kept available across the broader supply system and mobilized when needed. While the volume of supplies kept in company vegetable cellars has declined, the range of resources accessible through the supply chain has expanded. The change has not only eased the burden of winter preparations but also improved the freshness and variety of meals available to troops. An official from the Central Military Commission's Logistic Support Department told the Daily that efforts will continue to improve procurement and reserve mechanisms, integrating winter preparations, traditionally treated as a seasonal task, into the regular logistic support system.

item.title: Upgraded China-made autonomous mission management system to debut at Airshow China 2026
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 19:03:00
FH series UAVs are displayed at Airshow China 2021 in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province. Photo: Courtesy of China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation An upgraded version of China's domestically developed Hongshan autonomous mission management system will be unveiled at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, also known as Airshow China, which is set for December 7 to 13 in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province, China Space News reported on Monday evening. Unlike the debut of the original version at the 2024 airshow, where the system focused on demonstrations of coordinated drone swarm flights, the upgraded version expands its capabilities to integrated unmanned and counter-unmanned operations. It can connect different types of unmanned platforms and use AI algorithms to complete multiple tasks. Independently developed by the Aerospace Times Feihong Technology Co (ATFTC) under the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corp, the Hongshan system was designed to meet the demands of large-scale coordinated unmanned operations, said the report. Built on an open architecture for multi-agent coordination and management, the system can flexibly integrate different types of military and civilian unmanned platforms, including drones, unmanned ground vehicles and unmanned surface vessels. Taking into account mission objectives, environmental information and system capability models, it supports closed-loop operations, from the fusion of reconnaissance and intelligence to digital battlefield simulation, AI-generated strike plans and assessments of operational effectiveness. The company said the system offers clear situational awareness, rapid decision-making, effective control and traceability, with capabilities comparable to international counterparts and advantages in certain areas. During the exhibition, the company will set up a command-and-control center at the venue. Using satellite communications and drone data links, the system will establish a high-bandwidth, low-latency information network, enabling commands issued at Zhuhai Jinwan Airport to reach an aerospace base in the Damao Banner, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, about 2,600 kilometers away, almost instantly. From what has been seen so far, the Hongshan system seems to have overcome several long-standing challenges, including communication delays, differences in data formats across unmanned platforms, and the need for precise timing synchronization, all of which usually make real-time command and control over long distances difficult, Chinese military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times on Tuesday. Addressing these challenges requires a distributed architecture combining space, air and ground communication links with cloud-based computing. Autonomous decision-making capabilities at the remote end are also essential to compensate for satellite transmission delays and therefore maintain operational responsiveness, Song said. The Hongshan system's role as the "brain" of an unmanned operational network lies not only in its current capabilities but also in its potential for further development. At this year's airshow, its multi-agent coordination architecture will enable different types of unmanned equipment to autonomously form operational groups, share situational information and coordinate in response to changing conditions, completing the entire operational process through closed-loop simulation. The system will also allow new equipment and algorithms to be rapidly integrated, while continuously refining coordination strategies through data accumulated in operational confrontations. Meanwhile, the company has established an integration standards framework for unmanned operations that features a unified architecture, compatible interfaces, interoperable data and efficient coordination. It aims to break down data silos between equipment from different manufacturers and across different models, allowing various unmanned platforms to be integrated into the Hongshan system. Song said the system's interoperability could facilitate bringing previously fragmented unmanned platforms into an integrated network that can be coordinated across military services and dynamically reconfigured, turning the capabilities of individual platforms into broader operational advantages. This is where its real value lies. China Space News noted that unmanned combat forces have become a major development priority for the world's leading military powers, reshaping modern warfare and the rules of military confrontation. At the 13th Airshow China in 2021, the FH series included stealth drones, loitering munitions and integrated reconnaissance-strike UAVs. Among the products on display, two eye-catching ones were the FH-95 electronic warfare and armed reconnaissance UAV system and the FH-97 high-speed stealth drone. The FH-97 is a medium-range, high-speed UAV designed for rapid reconnaissance and surveillance, target positioning verification, artillery correction and damage assessment. The FH-95, meanwhile, is designed for all-weather, round-the-clock reconnaissance and surveillance missions. At that time, Chen Jianguo, then general manager and a researcher with ATFTC, said electronic warfare had become an essential component of modern warfare, with electronic warfare, reconnaissance and early-warning drones playing an increasingly important role. Such platforms can conduct remote detection beyond defensive perimeters or carry out tactical feints and saturation attacks in coordination with manned aircraft. At the 14th Airshow China in 2022, the FH-97A attracted attention for its resemblance to the J-20 stealth fighter. An upgraded version of the FH-97, the FH-97A has an electro-optical tracking and targeting system added to its nose, according to CCTV News. Designed for air combat, the UAV features stealth capabilities, high maneuverability, short takeoff and landing, reusability, radar evasion and decoy capabilities. It is designed to operate alongside manned stealth fighters in future combat scenarios, CCTV said. According to an introduction to Airshow China 2026, the Lianzhou unmanned equipment exhibition zone will serve as a platform for showcasing drones and counter-drone systems. Dynamic counter-drone demonstrations will be a major highlight, with participating companies presenting various countermeasures and their latest technological developments. Several new drone models will also take part in flight demonstrations.

item.title: Chinese PLA steps up joint training among Navy, Air Force and Rocket Force to strengthen integrated operational capabilities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 20:38:00
PLA Navy guided-missile destroyer Zibo sails on the sea. Photo: 81.cn The Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) is stepping up efforts to promote joint training among its military services, with a PLA Navy destroyer flotilla opening up its maritime training resources to Air Force and Rocket Force units, according to a report from the PLA Daily. Such efforts are seen as an important step toward building a world-class military by strengthening the PLA's joint operational capabilities and improving coordination among its services, experts noted. During a recent maritime exercise aboard the PLA Navy guided-missile destroyer Zibo , naval personnel identified gaps in their ability to detect very-low-altitude targets under certain sea conditions and electronic jamming scenarios. Air Force officer Wei Yufeng, drawing on his perspective as an aerial attacker, offered suggestions for improving the formation's air defense positioning and the timing of fire coordination, according to the PLA Daily report. Wei also served as a cross-service staff officer during the exercise, helping the ship's crew assess the air situation. His participation brought an Air Force perspective into the Navy's training and reviews, allowing naval personnel to examine their air-defense arrangements from the perspective of an aerial attacker. The waters were once used primarily by the Navy, but under an initiative to open up training to other services, Air Force aircraft and Rocket Force units have increasingly joined exercises in the area. Maritime training grounds are no longer used exclusively by the Navy but have become a shared venue where personnel from different services can train together, improve coordination and test their capabilities. The exercise gave personnel from the two services a better understanding of each other's capabilities and operational requirements. Previous joint exercises had exposed gaps in coordination, including difficulties in aligning air strikes with naval air-defense operations and directing timely strikes against maneuvering maritime targets, according to the report. To address these gaps, the task force has incorporated its annual training plan into a broader joint training program, reporting available maritime training areas and time slots, electromagnetic environments, simulated opposing forces and support resources to higher-level authorities for allocation. Other services can submit specific training requests, which a dedicated team then coordinates and integrates into joint exercises. Regular joint training has helped personnel better understand operational capabilities, an officer with a PLA Navy unit affiliated with the Eastern Theater Command told the PLA Daily. Air Force officers have learned about the detection limits of naval radar, while naval commanders have gained a better understanding of air-strike tactics and vulnerabilities, the officer said. The key to improving joint operations lies not only in upgrading equipment, but also in breaking down barriers over the use of training resources and making them serve broader operational needs, the officer said. "Modern warfare can break out at any time and in any place, including across different maritime areas. While the PLA previously needed a longer period to prepare for operations, that preparation time has now been significantly shortened. This reflects the continuous improvement and upgrading of its information systems and command structures," Song Zhongping, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times. According to Song, joint operations involving the Navy, Air Force and Rocket Force are particularly important because modern warfare cannot be fought by a single service acting alone. It requires different services to work together through integrated command and data-link systems. "There is still work to be done to further improve and upgrade these systems, ensuring that different services can operate on a unified data network and be brought together when needed to conduct joint operations across different domains, at any time and in any location. This is where the practical value of joint operations lies," noted Song. The initiative builds on a longer-term effort to integrate the PLA's forces and improve their ability to operate together. The effort is part of the PLA's broader push to strengthen joint operations. China's 2015 white paper on military strategy called for gradually establishing an integrated joint operational system, bringing different operational forces, units and elements together through information systems. The country has formulated a three-step development strategy for modernizing national defense and the armed forces, with the aim of achieving the centenary objectives of the PLA by 2027, basically realizing the modernization of national defense and the armed forces by 2035, and fully building the armed forces into world-class forces by the mid-21st century, according to the white paper. According to Song, the PLA has continued to make progress in strengthening its information capabilities and improving coordination among its military services. It is also making greater use of information and intelligent technologies to enhance its operational capabilities. "Further efforts are needed to deepen the integration of different services and build a more unified and efficient joint operational system," he said.

item.title: State media highlights military potential of China's domestically developed 7-ton-class large cargo drone
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 16:25:00
The fully domestically developed large cargo unmanned aerial vehicle NORINCO LUCA parks at a test flight site in Zhengzhou, Central China's Henan Province, on March 31, 2026. Photo: Liang Rui/GT Military affairs experts on a CCTV News military channel program on Sunday offered further analysis of the overall performance and advanced autonomous control capabilities of China's fully domestically developed NORINCO LUCA, a 7-ton-class large cargo unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), elaborating on its potential military applications. The drone recently completed its first cargo transport and airdrop test, with its developers highlighting its potential use in emergency response and disaster relief. Military commentator Wang Mingzhi highlighted several key features of the drone during the program, including its large payload capacity and long range. With a range of 3,000 kilometers and a payload capacity of 3.5 tons, the aircraft can deliver supplies over long distances with high efficiency. Wang also noted its strong environmental adaptability, saying that its short takeoff and landing capability allows it to operate from relatively simple runways, expanding the range of locations where it can take off and land. Another notable feature of the NORINCO LUCA is its straight-through cargo compartment, which makes loading and unloading highly efficient and convenient, Wang said. The ability to complete loading and unloading in a short time is particularly important not only in peacetime but also in wartime, he noted, as it allows supplies to be transferred and dispatched more rapidly, improving the efficiency of logistical operations. Cargo pallets loaded with goods in the straight-through cargo hold of the NORINCO LUCA. Photo: Courtesy of Norinco Group The Global Times learned from its developer, NORINCO UAS, a subsidiary of China's State-owned Norinco Group, that cargo pallets are automatically released from the aircraft according to preset commands. During the process, the onboard system automatically assesses the cargo loading status and manages flight trim, ensuring stable flight as the payload changes. These capabilities demonstrate the drone's technological advantages in unmanned and intelligent cargo transport and delivery missions. Wang said its high degree of autonomy, combined with a precision airdrop system, allows the drone to accurately deliver supplies to designated locations over long distances. It also has considerable potential for functional expansion, thanks to its modular design. In addition to its large cargo compartment, the aircraft is equipped with hardpoints under its wings, allowing different payloads to be configured according to mission requirements. This could enable it to evolve beyond a conventional cargo transport platform and undertake a wider range of missions, Wang said. Military commentator Wei Dongxu added in the interview that the drone could provide substantial logistical support during military operations. For instance, in island operations or amphibious landings, it could deliver supplies to beachhead positions. With a range of several thousand kilometers, the drone can cover the distances involved, while each aircraft can carry and deliver 3.5 tons of operational supplies, Wei said in the CCTV News program. According to NORINCO UAS, the first cargo transport and airdrop test covered the entire operational process, including cargo loading and inspection, flight-route programming, takeoff, cruise, cargo-door opening, automatic airdrop, parachute-line recovery, landing and assessment of the cargo's landing point. The ground control station monitored the flight and airdrop throughout the test. All systems operated normally, while data links remained stable, the developer said. The successful test came just eight months after the drone made its maiden flight. NORINCO UAS said it is the world's largest logistics cargo drone to have successfully completed a maiden flight. Several large logistics drones are under development or already in service internationally. NORINCO LUCA leads in key performance indicators including payload capacity, airdrop operating envelope, landing accuracy, short takeoff and landing capability, and product maturity, chief designer Geng Jianzhong told the Global Times previously. The development team said they will continue evaluating airdrop accuracy, timing control and system performance to support further upgrades, airworthiness certification and practical applications.

item.title: Expert expects debut of newly commissioned Type 055 as PLA Navy announces mysterious destroyer's participation in Airshow China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 16:15:00
The PLA Navy released a silhouette image, inviting the public to guess which "mysterious 10,000-tonne destroyer" will appear at the December airshow. The PLA Navy has unveiled a broad lineup of ships and aircraft for the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition (Airshow China 2026), stoking intrigue over a "mysterious 10,000-tonne destroyer" whose identity will be disclosed at the December event. A military affairs analyst told the Global Times that the vessel is likely a latest Type 055 destroyer, set for its public debut. Its planned public appearance would send a clear signal that the new warship has attained steady operational capability, as the ongoing commissioning of Type 055 hulls bolsters the navy's far-sea deployment and combat capacity. The 16th Airshow China will be held December 7 to 13 in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province. Breaking new ground, this edition adds a maritime display zone at Gaolan Port to bring a sea dimension to the expo. It will stage an integrated, panoramic display of the PLA Navy's main warships, next-generation carrier-based aircraft, Marine Corps assets and intelligent unmanned equipment across land, sea and air. Multiple active-duty systems will be unveiled publicly for the first time, illustrating the full scope of the People's Navy's transformation drive in the new era, according to a release the PLA Navy's WeChat account published on Monday. New mainstay vessels including the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, Type 055 guided-missile destroyer and Type 054A guided-missile frigate will be moored at Gaolan Port and open to visitors. In its guidance for booking vessel visits, the PLA Navy named the Type 075 Hubei and Type 054A Huangshan as confirmed participants. The Type 055 destroyer is framed instead as a "mysterious 10,000-tonne destroyer." "Its identity is not yet disclosed. Guess who I am — the answer comes in December," the release said. "This is very probably a latest Type 055 10,000-tonne destroyer, holding its first public appearance for the Airshow China in Zhuhai," Zhang Junshe, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Monday. The PLA Navy WeChat account also noted that this year's event will feature "a slate of next-generation assets that are newly commissioned, newly certified and newly combat-ready, alongside active-duty main warships." "The public showing of a fresh Type 055 destroyer is a direct display of the PLA Navy's openness, transparency and self-assurance," Zhang said, noting that exhibiting the new vessel also sends a clear message that it has achieved steady operational capability. Visitors to the airshow will get an up-close look at the large warship dockside and that visceral impression beats written descriptions, turning maritime defense strength into something visible and tangible and bolstering public faith in national security, according to the expert. "The arrival of this newest Type 055 destroyer epitomizes the PLA Navy's evolution from an offshore force to a far-sea navy, and highlights its resolve and wherewithal to uphold peace," Zhang said. Back in March, the PLA Navy released footage of the Type 055 guided-missile destroyers Dongguan , the ninth hull, and Anqing , the 10th, conducting combat training. That brought the total number of commissioned Type 055 10,000-tonne destroyers to 10. It means the "mysterious" large destroyer premiering at the airshow is likely to be the third Type 055 to enter service in 2026. Zhang said the commissioning of three Type 055 destroyers within a single year reflects China's maturing shipbuilding technology and craftsmanship and the establishment of a fully modern, complete shipbuilding ecosystem. "The first Type 055, the Nanchang , took roughly six years from keel-laying to commissioning. Construction timelines for later hulls have shortened markedly, showing that stable, mature workflows are now in place across design, construction, outfitting and sea trials. This rests on a robust, dependable supporting supply chain," said Zhang. The propulsion, radar, electronic systems and specialized materials required for these large destroyers can be delivered in sustained batches. Suppliers upstream can maintain steady delivery schedules, ensuring consistent build quality. The high degree of uniformity in the vessels' hull form and equipment arrangement also points to tightly controlled dimensional tolerances, reliable welding precision and well-established assembly standards, according to the expert. Three vessels in total will be featured at the Gaolan Port maritime display zone at the airshow, and the two confirmed ships already named belong to the Southern Theater Command Navy. "As a general rule, each theater command typically handles events within its own area of responsibility and does not routinely reallocate assets across theater boundaries," Zhang said, noting that means this "mysterious 10,000-tonne destroyer" is also likely assigned to the Southern Theater Command Navy. Public records show that among the 10 Type 055 destroyers unveiled so far, four are assigned to the Northern Theater Command Navy, four to the Southern Theater Command Navy and two to the Eastern Theater Command Navy. Zhang said one key consideration behind the possible stationing of the latest Type 055 with the South Sea fleet is escort duties for China's dual carrier strike groups. Both the Shandong and Fujian are homeported in the South China Sea. As the carrier's primary escort, the Type 055 is tasked with establishing long-range air defense, anti-missile and anti-submarine cover to round out the carrier group's configuration. The South China Sea's vast expanse, dotted with islands and reefs, carries high strategic value. It has a pressing need for frontline warships capable of sustained far-sea management to safeguard maritime zones and sea lanes. The Type 055's robust area air defense and multi-domain strike capabilities are well suited to operational requirements in the South China Sea, said Zhang. The expert also noted that the steady commissioning of additional Type 055 destroyers continues to strengthen the PLA Navy's overseas deployment and warfighting capacity. In peacetime, the navy can maintain regular large surface combatant deployments across multiple strategic axes, extending maritime early-warning coverage and boosting maritime and aerial surveillance. "Should contingencies arise, the service gains greater confidence for rapid response and emergency operations, with improved system-of-systems performance and faster capability generation," said the expert.

item.title: PLA Navy to debut JL-15 trainer aircraft, WZ-2 unmanned helicopter at Airshow China 2026
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 12:00:00
On the evening of November 1, 2026, a drone light performance lit up the sky over Zhuhai, Guangdong, kicking off pre-event celebrations marking the 77th founding anniversary of the PLA Air Force and the 30th anniversary of the Airshow China 2026. Photo: VCG The PLA Navy on Monday unveiled its lineup for the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition (Airshow China 2026). It will display the JL-15 trainer aircraft and WZ-2 unmanned helicopter to the public for the first time at the event. Under a coordinated arrangement, the PLA Navy will showcase a mix of actual hardware and scale models in four categories: indoor exhibitions, outdoor static displays, flight demonstrations and vessel open-house visits. The outdoor static display area will also feature new aircraft such as the J-15T carrier-based fighter, Z-20F carrier-borne anti-submarine helicopter, Y-9 anti-submarine patrol aircraft and WZ-2 unmanned helicopter, according to the PLA Navy. For the flight demonstrations, the PLA Navy will deploy the J-35 carrier-based stealth fighter jet and J-15T carrier-based heavy fighter, the KJ-600 early warning aircraft, along with the JL-15 trainer aircraft as well as Z-20J and Z-8C helicopters. They will perform formation flypasts, low-level passes and airfield raid drills, offering a multi-dimensional, three-dimensional showcase of the PLA Navy's maritime and aerial combat system. All three surface combatants at the Gaolan Port maritime exhibition zone - the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, Type 055 large destroyer and Type 054A frigate - are making their Airshow China debut. Among the aerial contingent, the J-35, KJ-600, Z-20F, Y-9 anti-submarine patrol aircraft, JL-15 and WZ-2 unmanned helicopter are also first-time participants at the expo, according to the PLA Navy.

item.title: Type 075, Type 055 and Type 054A warships to open to public at 16th Airshow China: PLA Navy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 11:20:00
Up: The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy's Type 075 amphibious assault ship Hubei Photo: PLA Southern Theater Command Down left: A Type 054A frigate Down right: A Type 055 destroyer Photos: VCG The PLA Navy on Monday released its lineup for the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition (Airshow China 2026), which includes the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 large destroyer and the Type 054A frigate. Experts on military affairs told the Global Times that the star-studded display features three major highlights: the "five carrier-related assets," nearly 10 types of new main combat equipment, and a combined display of surface vessels, carrier-based jets and marine forces, showcasing the navy's systemic combat prowess. Under a coordinated arrangement, the PLA Navy will showcase a mix of actual hardware and scale models in four categories: indoor exhibitions, outdoor static displays, flight demonstrations and vessel open-house visits. The exhibits will include main combat warships, carrier-based fighter jets, carrier-borne helicopters, anti-submarine patrol aircraft, shipborne weapon systems and armored equipment, according to the PLA Navy. New-generation main combat vessels, including the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 guided-missile destroyer and the Type 054A guided-missile frigate, will be open to the public at Gaolan Port. The outdoor static display area will also feature new aircraft such as the J-15T carrier-based fighter, the Z-20F carrier-borne anti-submarine helicopter, the Y-9 anti-submarine patrol aircraft and the WZ-2 unmanned helicopter. For the flight demonstrations, the PLA Navy will deploy the J-35 carrier-based stealth fighter jet, the J-15T carrier-based heavy fighter, the KJ-600 early warning aircraft, and the JL-15 trainer aircraft, as well as the Z-20J and Z-8C helicopters. They will perform formation flypasts, low-level passes and airfield raid drills, offering a multi-dimensional showcase of the PLA Navy's maritime and aerial combat system. Thirty years have passed since the China Airshow was first held in Zhuhai in 1996. The PLA Navy brought physical equipment to the 15th Airshow for the first time in 2024. This year's edition marks the launch of a new offshore exhibition zone at Gaolan Port, where a large formation of active-duty naval vessels is set to be on display, according to experts. "For the first time, this Airshow opens the offshore exhibition area at Gaolan Port, where the PLA Navy's main combat ships will make their debut at the Zhuhai Airshow. Its greatest significance lies in breaking the previous limitation of the Airshow, which largely focused on aerial hardware, enabling the simultaneous display of naval, land, air and space equipment," Zhang Junshe, a military affairs expert told the Global Times on Monday. Previous editions of the Airshow focused primarily on aerial assets. The newly added naval vessel segment fills a critical gap in the maritime dimension, delivering a more comprehensive exhibition framework. Visitors can get up close to active-duty warships and book tours on board, offering a more immersive, firsthand viewing experience than past displays, which were limited to scale models, said Zhang. "The concentrated participation of naval equipment further broadens the international profile of Airshow China in Zhuhai and elevates its global standing. It also fully demonstrates China's robust capacity to host a large-scale defense expo covering land, sea, air and space domains," the expert said. All three surface combatants at the Gaolan Port maritime exhibition zone - the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 large destroyer and the Type 054A frigate - are making their debut at Airshow China. Among the aerial contingent, the J-35, KJ-600, Z-20F, Y-9 anti-submarine patrol aircraft, JL-15 and WZ-2 unmanned helicopter are also participating in the expo for the first time. Compared to the PLA Navy's debut at Airshow China in 2024, the navy is fielding three types of main combat warships and nearly 10 types of aircraft this year, forming an exceptionally strong lineup, Zhang said. Zhang outlined three standout highlights of the naval display. Topping the list is the first-ever public tour of the Type 055 10,000-ton-class destroyer. As China's first domestically built destroyer of this displacement class, the vessel is known as the "sword-bearing guard" for carrier strike groups. It incorporates breakthroughs in overall design and information integration. As a landmark platform symbolizing China's transition from offshore defense to far-sea operations, it stands among the world's most capable surface combatants. The second highlight is the complete lineup of the "five carrier-related assets" on show in Zhuhai. The suite includes the J-35 stealth carrier-based fighter, catapult-launched J-15T multirole carrier fighter, KJ-600 carrier-borne early warning aircraft, J-15DT carrier-based electronic warfare jet and Z-20F carrier anti-submarine helicopter. Third, unmanned systems headlined by the WZ-2 unmanned helicopter are appearing alongside unmanned surface vessels and other unmanned hardware. Taken together, these three highlights offer a comprehensive picture of the PLA Navy's evolving capabilities in far-sea defense, system-of-systems warfare and intelligent unmanned operations. The guided-missile destroyer Dalian (Hull 105) attached to the PLA Southern Theater Command sails during a far-sea joint training drill in early April, 2023. Photo: eng.chinamil.com.cn "The J-35, KJ-600 and Z-20F are all making their debut at Airshow China. Among them, the Z-20F carrier-based anti-submarine helicopter is appearing at an airshow for the first time and is being unveiled to the public for the very first time. This marks the public debut of all five domestically developed carrier-related assets," said Zhang, adding that the completion of this carrier-based aviation system will further strengthen the overall combat capabilities of China's carrier strike groups. According to official information, compared with previous airshow, the PLA Navy is placing greater emphasis on combat-oriented training this time. All exhibited items are active-duty main combat assets that regularly operate in the open ocean, carrying out combat readiness training, exercises and maritime rights protection missions. These are not static exhibits but warfighting hardware operating across the blue waters, vividly demonstrating the PLA Navy's operational readiness. The exhibition also highlights new-quality capabilities and emerging domains. It showcases a suite of next-generation platforms that have just entered service, received design certification or attained initial operational capability. The concentrated display of active-duty main warships offers a direct glimpse of the navy's robust open-ocean combat strength, testifying to the accelerated transformation of the navy amid the drive to strengthen the military in the new era. Systemic integration is another key focus. For the first time, the complete "vessel platform plus carrier-based aviation" system is presented together. Multiple newly upgraded and newly developed carrier-based fighters, early warning aircraft and helicopters make their collective debut. Displayed alongside major destroyers and frigates, amphibious warfare assets and coastal-sea defense systems, they illustrate the full maritime-air combat architecture of a carrier strike group. Greater prominence is also given to unmanned and intelligent systems. Unmanned aerial vehicles, unmanned underwater vehicles and other unmanned platforms and scale models will be on display, reflecting the PLA Navy's cutting-edge research into unmanned and intelligent warfare and pointing to emerging modes of future maritime combat.

item.title: Portable 'Wi-Fi' terminals help China's military units maintain battlefield connectivity on the move
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:11:00
Photo: PLA Daily A lightweight communication terminal, weighing less than 3 kilograms, is helping Chinese military units maintain communication links - like a portable Wi-Fi - as they maneuver between battlefield positions, offering a more flexible alternative to the time-consuming deployment of traditional communication cables, read a PLA Daily report on Sunday. The portable network and communications terminal, developed by a unit of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) Information Support Force, can be rapidly deployed to establish wireless connections between command terminals and frontline units, allowing information to be transmitted without waiting for communication cables to be laid again after a position change. In a recent joint training exercise, a PLA Air Force firepower unit received an order to relocate shortly after having completed a round of live-fire exercises. While a communications support team was preparing to carry conventional fiber-optic cables to the new position, an advance team reported that the portable terminal had already been set up, with the command communications link established. By the time the cable-laying team arrived, the firepower unit had completed a simulated strike and was preparing to move again, the PLA Daily reported. The development addresses a long-standing challenge in battlefield communications support. Under traditional arrangements, communications personnel had to retrieve and re-deploy cables whenever combat units changed positions, a process that required considerable manpower and time and could leave units temporarily without communications. Military commentator Song Zhongping told the Global Times on Sunday that mobile networking can significantly improve the speed and flexibility of communications support compared with conventional cable-based deployment. "Mobile networking, as the name suggests, means no longer having to lay extensive networks of cables as was traditionally done. The traditional approach consumes considerable manpower, material resources and financial resources, while its efficiency and ability to respond rapidly are limited," Song told the Global Times. By deploying mobile communications equipment, including base stations, military units can establish communications and command networks more quickly and move these capabilities to areas where they are needed, Song noted. "For a military force to respond rapidly, what needs to come first is not just logistics, but also command and communications," Song said. "Without that, it is impossible to achieve connectivity and interoperability across the entire force." According to the PLA Daily report, the portable terminals can be deployed at multiple locations to form a mobile networking cluster, rather than relying on a single communications node or fixed position. During another training exercise involving the seizure of key positions, an advance unit maneuvered through difficult terrain and areas with dense electromagnetic interference. Using multiple portable terminals, the unit established a mobile network while moving and filled gaps in communications coverage. When a reconnaissance team identified a simulated enemy firepower position, target information was transmitted through the mobile network to several dispersed firepower units. The units then coordinated their simulated strikes based on a shared, real-time operational picture. The communications links remained operational throughout the exercise, the PLA Daily report said. Song said the use of multiple interconnected nodes can improve the resilience of battlefield communications by providing redundancy. "Communications on the battlefield cannot rely entirely on a single node. Multiple nodes are needed, with several portable mobile communications terminals deployed redundantly to ensure that the entire communications network remains secure and reliable," Song told the Global Times. However, the shift toward wireless networking also brings security challenges that cannot be overlooked. Song noted that wireless communications inevitably involve the transmission of radio signals, creating the possibility that communications could be intercepted or information disclosed. Encryption and other security safeguards are therefore essential to mobile military communications systems. "How to prevent information from being leaked is the core challenge facing mobile and network-based communications," he said. The PLA Daily report also stressed that the portable terminals are not intended to replace wired communications. Instead, the unit is exploring a complementary model combining fixed and mobile systems: Wired networks are used at established positions, where reliability and resistance to interference are priorities, while portable equipment is deployed for temporary maneuvers and field operations, where rapid setup and filling coverage gaps are more important. The unit has also incorporated challenging conditions, including strong electromagnetic interference and difficult terrain, into routine training to test equipment performance and refine its networking methods. Looking ahead, Song said military communications systems would continue to evolve alongside advances in technology, with more sophisticated encryption methods and new forms of portable, distributed communications equipment potentially improving their security and reliability. "New technologies will continue to replace older ones, but the ultimate goal remains ensuring that communications are reliable and secure, with security always coming first," he said.
